source_read: PMC full text PMC3069146 (NIH author manuscript NIHMS258354; final version Drug Alcohol Depend 2011;115(1-2):120-130). Whole article read with get_page_text in my own tab (text saved locally); Tables 1-4 extracted cell by cell from the page's HTML to check column alignment; Figure 1 viewed on its figure page; author information and footnotes read (the manuscript has no funding, acknowledgment or competing-interest statement). Online supplementary tables 5 and 6 not read. Before this reading I had seen two of the card's values (8.9% without intervals; adjusted HR 0.63 for onset before 14) quoted in the Curran card's notes during the blind round; both are also in the claim statements.

claims.overstatement: Two small wording points. (1) 'With a median of about 5 years from first use to dependence': the source says half of the cases of cannabis dependence were observed about 5 years after first use, i.e. a median among those who became dependent, not among everyone who used. (2) The lead sentence says about 9 in 100 'had at some point met criteria'; that fits the NCS figure, but the NESARC 8.9% is a life-table projection of how many would become dependent at some time in life (the body of the claim words it correctly).
claims.note: All numbers confirmed: 7,389 cannabis users (abstract; Methods 2.1); 8.9%, 5.9% at a decade, 'almost 2.0%' after the first year (given jointly for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis), 67.5%, 22.7%, 20.9%, and half of cannabis cases about 5 years after first use (Results 3.3). The cumulative figures are projections from the standard actuarial method, with no intervals in the text or in Figure 1. Wave 2 is dated 2004-2005 in the text; the Wave 1 dates (2001-2002) appear only in a reference title. The sample is the 34,653 Wave 1 respondents re-interviewed at Wave 2 (of 43,093), so people who died between waves (1,403) are not included; Wave 2 response is not stated (editors' calculation: about 87% of the eligible). Not in the claim: the lifetime projection varied by racial-ethnic group from 8.2% (White) to 15.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander), log-rank 17.57, p < 0.01; and the paper calls its 5.9% at a decade consistent with the NCS estimate it cites as 8% (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Reporting inconsistencies: the cannabis subgroup counts in Tables 1 and 2 sum to 7,409, not 7,389; Table 2 counts 564 users with lifetime cannabis dependence while Tables 3-4 give N = 529.

anchors.extracted: Lifetime users of nicotine (15,918), alcohol (28,907), cannabis (7,389) and cocaine (2,259) who took part in both NESARC waves; discrete-time survival analyses. Cumulative probability of transition to dependence 67.5% nicotine, 22.7% alcohol, 20.9% cocaine, 8.9% cannabis; half of cases observed about 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after first use.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods › 2.1 Sample and procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Wave 2 NESARC 2004-2005; target population civilian non-institutionalized adults 18+ in households and group quarters, with Blacks, Hispanics and 18-24-year-olds oversampled; of 43,093 Wave 1 respondents, 34,653 re-interviewed at Wave 2 (deceased 1,403, impaired 781 and military 950 not eligible); weights adjust for Wave 2 non-response; analysis sample 7,389 lifetime cannabis users.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods › 2.2 Data collection, 1st paragraph; 2.3 Measures › 2.3.1 Substance use and dependence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: AUDADIS-IV structured interview; DSM-IV diagnoses by computer algorithm from Wave 1 (prevalent) and Wave 2 (incident between waves) data; dependence = 3 or more of 7 criteria within 12 months; cannabis use and age at first use self-reported; test-retest reliability of substance use disorder diagnoses kappa 0.54-0.91.

Projected cumulative probabilities of transition within the first year, the first decade and lifetime estimated by the standard actuarial method (SAS PROC LIFETEST); log-rank tests across substances and racial-ethnic groups. No intervals reported for these projections.

anchors.locator: 3. Results › 3.3 Probability of transitioning to substance dependence among substance users, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
anchors.extracted: After the first year: almost 2.0% for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis users (cocaine 7.1%); a decade after first use: cannabis 5.9% (nicotine 15.6%, cocaine 14.8%, alcohol 11.0%); lifetime: 8.9% of cannabis users would become dependent (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); half of the cannabis dependence cases observed about 5 years after first use. Figure 1 shows the four curves without intervals and without a key to the symbols.

anchors.locator: 3. Results › 3.3.3 Racial differences in transition to cannabis dependence, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Lifetime transition among cannabis users: White 8.2%, Black 9.7%, Hispanic 10.0%, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander 15.9%, American Indian or Alaska Native 14.8% (log-rank 17.57, p < 0.01); half of cases about 5 years after first use (about 10 years in the Pacific Islander group).

anchors.locator: Table 1 and Table 2, Cannabis Use column
anchors.extracted: Header N = 7,389, but subgroup counts sum to 7,409 (e.g. men 3,919 + women 3,490); 564 cannabis users with a lifetime cannabis dependence diagnosis (Table 2) against N = 529 cannabis dependence cases in Tables 3-4.

Authors call the decade estimates consistent with NCS estimates (Wagner & Anthony, 2002), which the Introduction gives as 8% cannabis dependence within a decade of first use, against 5.9% here; lifetime projections repeated.

Limitations: self-reported use and disorders not confirmed objectively; recall bias increasing with time since the event; intermittent use makes time from first use to dependence inexact; NESARC excludes institutionalized people, who are more likely to have dependence.

claims.overstatement: None material. Two precision points: (1) 'stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances' describes a model chosen by stepwise selection; for cannabis it kept sex, age group at interview and race-ethnicity (no income, education, marital, employment or nativity term), mood, anxiety and personality disorders, and nicotine, alcohol and cocaine dependence; (2) the authors' reading is hedged (transition 'may not be a consequence of early substance use onset per se').
claims.note: Numbers confirmed: before 14 against at or after 14 (Methods 2.3.3; Table 2), unadjusted HR 2.47 (95% CI 2.0-3.1, Table 3), adjusted 0.63 (0.5-0.9, Table 4); in the adjusted cannabis model mood disorder 2.69 (1.9-3.9), anxiety disorder 2.31 (1.6-3.4), personality disorder 2.3 (1.7-3.1), alcohol dependence 2.55 (1.8-3.5), cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6), and also nicotine dependence 2.06 (1.4-3.1), male sex 1.44, age 18-29 against 45+ 3.09. Column alignment checked in the page's table HTML. Unweighted, 1,051 cannabis users started before 14 and 6,339 at or after 14. Not in the claim and worth a clause: mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates, so the adjusted estimate also conditions on disorders that may follow early use; the reversal therefore does not show that early onset itself protects, which the claim does not say but a reader might infer. The authors also suggest later starters may have more intense use and easier access in late adolescence. The source measured neither frequency of use nor THC.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods › 2.3 Measures › 2.3.3 Demographic and other substance use-related variables, 1st paragraph; Table 2, 'Specific SU onset' rows, Cannabis Use column
anchors.extracted: Early onset defined as first use before age 14 (substance-specific); 1,051 cannabis users started before 14 and 6,339 at or after 14 (unweighted).

Univariate and multivariable discrete-time survival analyses, person-years from first use to dependence onset or Wave 2 interview; education, marital status, mood and anxiety disorders and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates; independent correlates chosen by stepwise selection on likelihood-ratio tests; Wave 2 weights; Taylor series standard errors.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Cannabis Dependence column (N = 529), row 'Specific SU onset (before age 14)'
anchors.extracted: Unadjusted HR for first cannabis use before 14: 2.47 (95% CI 2.0-3.1).

Adjusted (stepwise-selected) model: first use before 14 HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.5-0.9); male 1.44 (1.1-1.9); age 18-29 3.09 (1.9-4.9) and 30-44 2.46 (1.7-3.5) against 45+; American Indian or Alaska Native 1.91 (1.2-3.0); mood disorder 2.69 (1.9-3.9); anxiety disorder 2.31 (1.6-3.4); personality disorder 2.3 (1.7-3.1); nicotine dependence 2.06 (1.4-3.1); alcohol dependence 2.55 (1.8-3.5); cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6). Nativity, education, income, marital and employment status, psychotic disorder and family history not retained.

anchors.locator: 3. Results › 3.4 Predictors › 3.4.2 Psychopathological and substance use-related predictors, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: People who first used cannabis or cocaine before 14 were less likely to become dependent in the adjusted models; for nicotine, onset before 14 went with higher hazards.

Unadjusted, early onset went with higher risk, as in earlier studies; after controlling for socio-economic, psychiatric and drug-use covariates the direction changed for cannabis and cocaine, which the authors read as the higher risk being mostly explained by those factors, so transition may not result from early onset per se but from concomitant psychiatric and substance use disorders; later starters may also have more intense use and greater availability in late adolescence.
Self-report without objective confirmation, recall bias, intermittent use making timing inexact, and exclusion of institutionalized people.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed; Figure 1 also shows the curves without intervals.
Confirmed; the source's wording is 'almost 2.0%', given jointly for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis.

Numbers right, meaning to be stated: the source says half of the cases of dependence were observed about 27 (nicotine), 13 (alcohol), 5 (cannabis) and 4 (cocaine) years after first use, i.e. medians among people who became dependent, read from Figure 1, not the time by which half of users became dependent. The note on subgroup medians is confirmed (see reporting issue 3).

Confirmed (Tables 3-4; Results 3.4.2, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph; 51 cocaine users before 14 in Table 2). For cannabis, 1,051 users started before 14 and 6,339 at or after 14 (unweighted). Worth adding: the reversal follows adjustment for mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates, which may follow early use.
Recomputed from unweighted Table 2 counts: 50.7%, 30.7%, 80.5% and 92.7%.

Confirmed. The 80.4% counts the deceased (1,403), impaired (781) and military (950) as losses; among those known to be eligible, re-interview was about 86.7% (editors' calculation; the number deported is not given). The paper states no response rate.

reporting_issues.note: Issue confirmed (every Table 1 stratification sums to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263). The consequence's inference is not supported: the Discussion's rounded shares (one third, half, more than 80%, 90%) cannot tell such close denominators apart, and Table 2's onset rows sum to 7,390 for cannabis and 2,259 for cocaine, matching the stated Ns, but to 16,053 and 29,160 for nicotine and alcohol. The extra 20 cannabis users may be people without a usable age of onset; the paper does not say.
Confirmed. Nicotine fits the same pattern: overall about 27 years against 23 for White people, with only the Black group (30) above it.
Confirmed; Figure 1 has no intervals either.

Confirmed (Table 4 cocaine column blank for sex and age). Related: Results 3.4.1 says people under 45 were more likely to transition for any of the substances, which Table 4 does not show for cocaine.
Confirmed by a search of the whole page: author affiliations, notes and footnotes only.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary moderate, fits the cumulative transition probabilities that cl_can_dependence_how_many uses. The cannabis onset claim now uses the paper's hazard ratios, an exposure association; for that use a ROBINS-E appraisal would be needed (confounding; time-varying psychiatric and substance use disorders as possible mediators; survivors only; recalled onset ages), which this card does not provide.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor overall. One gap matters for the cannabis claims: the Discussion reads the reversal of early onset as the higher risk being 'mostly explained by' psychiatric and substance use covariates, treating time-varying disorders that may follow early use as confounders; and it cites socio-economic adjustment, though the cannabis model retained no socioeconomic term. Also, results_show says family history predicted transition across substances; in the adjusted models it was retained only for nicotine and alcohol.

missed: The cannabis column of Table 4 in full: male 1.44 (1.1-1.9); age 18-29 3.09 (1.9-4.9) and 30-44 2.46 (1.7-3.5) against 45+; American Indian or Alaska Native 1.91 (1.2-3.0); mood 2.69 (1.9-3.9); anxiety 2.31 (1.6-3.4); personality 2.3 (1.7-3.1); nicotine dependence 2.06 (1.4-3.1); alcohol 2.55 (1.8-3.5); cocaine 4.14 (2.3-7.6); onset before 14 0.63 (0.5-0.9). Nativity, education, income, marital and employment status, psychotic disorder and family history were not retained, so no socioeconomic term was in the model behind the reversal.
The Discussion's own alternative for the onset reversal (7th paragraph): people who start later may have more intense use and greater availability, affordability and acceptance in late adolescence.
The paper calls its 5.9% at a decade consistent with the NCS estimate, which its Introduction gives as 8% for cannabis within a decade (Wagner & Anthony, 2002).
Figure 1 in this manuscript has no key to its symbols; the curves can be identified only by matching their plateaus with the text.
Methods 2.1 lists the deceased, deported, impaired and military as 'eligible' where ineligible is evidently meant; the Wave 1 dates (2001-2002) appear only in a reference title, not in the text.
